headline: White House Now Literally Runs on Podcast Recommendations
subheadline: When your nation's AI policy is authored by venture capitalists with a Spotify feed, you've achieved peak capture.
source_headline: The All-In-ification of Trump's AI agenda
body_html:
We have officially entered the era where U.S. artificial intelligence policy is being authored in real-time by the hosts of a venture capital podcast. The "All-In" network—a collection of tech investors who built their fortunes by telling each other how visionary they are, three times weekly—has achieved what generations of lobbyists could only dream of: a direct pipeline into the Oval Office that bypasses Congress, the agency apparatus, and any pretense of democratic process. President Trump's accelerationist AI doctrine now bears the unmistakable fingerprints of people whose professional incentive is to move fast, break regulations, and capture regulatory arbitrage before the next funding round closes.

For those fortunate enough to have missed it, the "All-In" podcast is a gathering of high-net-worth tech entrepreneurs and investors who discuss startups, markets, and their own intellectual prowess with the self-seriousness usually reserved for central bank governors. Their network has now expanded beyond weekly episode recordings into something far more dangerous: direct ideological feeding tubes into White House policy development. This isn't lobbying in the traditional sense—there are no disclosure forms, no official titles, no paper trail of campaign contributions that require reporting. Instead, it's the softer, more insidious version: a marriage of convenience between MAGA's anti-establishment impulses and Silicon Valley's anti-regulatory fervor, each side convinced it's using the other, neither realizing they've already merged.

The durability of this unlikely alliance is worth examining, because it reveals something broken in how American governance currently functions. These tech investors don't need traditional lobbying infrastructure anymore. They have something better: a media platform with an audience that includes the President, and enough credibility within their bubble to make their policy preferences sound like inevitable technological truths rather than financial interests masquerading as principle. When your preferred policy gets transmitted to power through a podcast episode rather than a regulatory comment period, you've achieved a form of capture so complete it barely requires concealment.

What makes this particular arrangement so exquisitely dystopian is the language of inevitability surrounding it. The narrative being floated is that this marriage was "unlikely" and has "proved remarkably durable"—as if it were a surprise that people with billions of dollars in AI holdings would develop aligned incentives with the administration controlling AI regulation. It's the same rhetorical sleight of hand that presents venture capital as meritocratic, or suggests that when founders fund political movements, they're motivated by principle rather than tax policy. The "All-In" network isn't whispering ideas into the White House because they're uniquely wise; they're there because their wealth buys access that ordinary citizens cannot afford.

The downstream consequences are already foreseeable. When your nation's AI policy is being shaped by people whose primary experience is raising venture capital and exiting companies at favorable valuations, you get policy designed to maximize the financial returns of early-stage AI firms rather than public safety, labor protection, or any regulatory framework that might interfere with explosive growth. The accelerationist doctrine isn't an accident—it's a business model. These investors have already bought their AI chips, funded their AI startups, and positioned their portfolios for an environment with minimal safety guardrails and maximum upside capture.

This is what regulatory capture looks like in the 2020s: not smoke-filled rooms with K Street fixers, but a podcast feed with venture capitalists who've successfully convinced a President that their financial interests are synonymous with national technological destiny. The truly genius part is that most of the people involved probably believe it.
glossary_definition: A euphemism for complete ideological alignment when both parties stand to profit enormously from the same deregulatory outcome.
